Add a buffer. A 10–20% margin covers slow months, late payments and unplanned costs. Without it, one quiet quarter puts you behind for the year.
Add business expenses. Software subscriptions, hardware, insurance, coworking, accountant fees, marketing, courses. These are paid by your business before you see a cent.

Billable hours per day. Developers who track time honestly land between four and six billable hours on a good day. Code review, Slack, estimates and context-switching eat the rest. Enter five, not eight.
Count your billable hours honestly. Billable hours per day × working days per week × (52 − weeks off). Five billable hours a day, five days a week and six weeks off is 1,150 hours — not 2,080.
Creatives with lots of short bookings should keep weeks off generous to cover the gaps.
Divide. Gross revenue needed ÷ billable hours = your minimum hourly rate. Everything above it is profit; anything below means you are subsidising your clients.
Editing and rewrites: charge hourly; scope is impossible to predict from a word count.
Employer payroll taxes. In the US the employer's half of Social Security and Medicare is 7.65 percent of salary; as a contractor you pay both halves. Raise the tax rate field accordingly.
Equipment, software and training that used to arrive on your desk.
Expenses. Hosting for demos, a good machine every three years, paid APIs, courses, an accountant, coworking. $4,000 to $8,000 a year is normal; add health insurance if you pay it yourself.
General admin (inbox, calendar, data entry, travel) sits at the lower end of VA rates.
Give notice. 30–60 days is standard; announce the new rate for work starting after a specific date.
Gross it up for taxes. Divide the take-home goal by (1 − tax rate). At a 25% effective rate, keeping $60,000 requires $80,000 of pre-tax profit.
Hardware: a colour-accurate monitor, a tablet and a machine that renders without stalling, replaced every three to four years.
Health insurance for an individual commonly costs $5,000 to $9,000 a year without a subsidy, more for a family. Put it in expenses.
Hourly for open-ended work: re-cuts, feedback-heavy corporate projects, assisting on someone else's edit.

Hourly is transparent and protects you when scope is unclear, but it caps your income at hours worked and penalises efficiency. Project (fixed) pricing is easier for clients to say yes to and lets you earn more as you get faster, provided you scope carefully and price in revision rounds. Retainers — a fixed monthly fee for ongoing availability or a block of hours — smooth your cash flow and are usually priced with a small discount in exchange for commitment. Many freelancers use all three: hourly for discovery and maintenance, fixed fees for defined deliverables, retainers for long-term clients. Whatever the model, your hourly floor from this calculator is the number no quote should fall below.
IT contractors on long engagements can set hours to 7.5 or 8 and reduce weeks off, since utilisation is high.
Keep it short and confident. A two-paragraph email beats a long justification. Most clients expect periodic increases.
Lead with value, not costs. Mention results delivered and expanded skills rather than your rent going up.
Licences you buy per project that clients rarely reimburse: typefaces, mockups, illustration packs.
Long-form and technical pieces with expert interviews: 10 to 20 hours per 2,000 words.

Monthly packages (for example 20 hours a month, paid in advance) are how experienced VAs stabilise income. Price them at your hourly rate times the hours, with a small discount for prepayment and a clear policy for unused and extra hours.
Offer a path. A retainer or prepaid block at a slightly lower rate makes the increase easier to accept.
Paid time off. Twenty days of holiday plus public holidays and sick days is five to six weeks you no longer earn during; that is the weeks-off field.

Per finished minute for predictable formats. Time a few past jobs: a talking-head YouTube video often needs 1 to 2 hours per finished minute; motion-heavy social ads can need 4 to 8. Multiply by your rate.
Per project for packages (a wedding film, a course of ten lessons) with a stated number of revision rounds and extra rounds billed hourly.
Portfolio and promotion: domain, hosting, printed samples, the odd awards entry.
Production crews often work ten-hour days: set billable hours per day to 10 so the day rate reflects it, and put overtime terms in writing.
Raise with new clients first. Test the new rate on fresh proposals, then bring existing clients up to it.
Retirement match of 3 to 6 percent of salary disappears unless you fund it yourself.
Short, researched content (blog posts, newsletters): expect 4 to 8 hours per 1,000 words including revisions.
Software: Creative Cloud, Figma, font services and stock subscriptions add up to $1,000 to $2,500 a year on their own.

Specialised support such as bookkeeping, podcast production, social media management, CRM administration or customer support in a second language commands 30 to 100 percent more, because it replaces a specialist, not an assistant.
Start with your take-home goal. This is what you want to actually keep each year — the equivalent of a net salary.
Taxes and buffer. Self-employment tax plus income tax commonly takes 25 to 35 percent in the US. The buffer covers the quiet month between contracts and the client who pays 60 days late.

Published "average freelance rates" vary enormously by country, specialty, seniority and how the survey was run, so treat them as context, not a target. This calculator does not use benchmark data; it computes the rate your numbers require. If the result is far above what your market pays, the fix is usually to raise billable efficiency, lower expenses, specialise, or target clients with bigger budgets — not to accept a rate that cannot sustain you.
